is a programming language and idea that has been bouncing around my head since 2015 in different forms. Every single feature of the language arose from pushing the type system of existing languages to their limits. I was programming and I ran into some limitation and wanted something that didn’t exist. I am definitely a craftsperson over an academic. Most of the things concepts were things I’ve been bouncing around my head for a while without concern for the underlying computer science behind it. It is most heavily influenced by C# followed closely by Typescript with a sprinkling of Haskell. While many other language may have the same features it is not derived from them, and then instead more of a coincidence, and consequently deviated without concern.","breadcrumbs":"Introduction » Introduction","id":"0","title":"Introduction"},"1":{"body":"C# Foundation - When in doubt default to the C# way of doing things. Assume if it’s part of C# it has a place in Mist. Anything removed or modified must have a rationale on why it doesn’t belong. If something in Mist is semantiaclly the same as C# we should default to the C# syntax. When introducing new concepts we should respect the C# origin as much as possible. A C# developer should be able to self discover how the features work. Comptime Focused - I strongly believe that the purpose of a programming language is to allow for the programmer to express guarentees that they want the compiler to enforce at compile time so that they do not need to reason about it at runtime. With that in mind all new features should be things that can reasoned about at comptime. We aim to make taking unproven actions comptime errors and couple with a type system to arm the developer to express this properly. Composable - Language features should be building blocks that interact and compose with other language features. We should be weary of islands of functionality that exist on their own. Conservative Keywords - Less is more when it comes to keywords. We should be hestitant to introduce new keywords when existing ones can be leveraged. A new keyword should signal something that is a novel addition from something C# can do to help bring attention that there is no parallel in the parent language.","breadcrumbs":"Introduction » Tenets","id":"1","title":"Tenets"},"10":{"body":"The simplest way to use Mist during development. Build the CLI project and invoke it through dotnet run: Clone the Mist repository: git clone https://github.com/mist-lang/mist.git\\ncd mist Build the CLI project: dotnet build Source/Mist.CLI/Mist.CLI.csproj -c Release Run the compiler using dotnet run, passing arguments after --: dotnet run --project Source/Mist.CLI -- build ./my-project\\ndotnet run --project Source/Mist.CLI -- run ./my-project This approach requires the .NET SDK on every invocation but needs no installation or PATH changes.","breadcrumbs":"Installation » Option A: Build and Run via dotnet run","id":"10","title":"Option A: Build and Run via dotnet run"},"100":{"body":"Arrays in Mist are fixed-size, bounds-checked collections. Unlike many languages where arrays are simple contiguous buffers with unchecked access, Mist arrays carry their size in the type system and the compiler statically proves that every index access is within bounds.","breadcrumbs":"Arrays » Arrays","id":"100","title":"Arrays"},"101":{"body":"The underlying array type is Array<T, Length> from the Standard Library, where Length is a dependent type parameter constrained to be a non-negative integer. In practice you’ll use shorthand syntax: Syntax Meaning int[5] Array<int, 5> — an array of exactly 5 ints int[] Array<int, unknown> — an array of ints whose length is not statically known var arr = new int[5] Compiler infers int[5] — the size is known var arr = [1, 2, 3] Compiler infers int[3] from the literal The T[] form is shorthand for Array<T, unknown> — the length exists but isn’t statically known in this context. The T[N] form tracks the exact size at compile time.","breadcrumbs":"Arrays » The Array Type","id":"101","title":"The Array Type"},"102":{"body":"Array indexing uses a refinement type called ArrayBounds defined as >= 0 and < Length. The compiler must prove that any index expression satisfies this constraint at compile time. If it can’t, the code won’t compile. This means: Literal indices on known-size arrays are checked at compile time Loop induction variables bounded by .Length are proven safe automatically Arbitrary expressions that can’t be proven safe are rejected The details of how this works are covered in the Refinement Types and Dependent Types chapters. For practical purposes: use standard for loop patterns with .Length and the compiler handles the rest.","breadcrumbs":"Arrays » Bounds Checking","id":"102","title":"Bounds Checking"},"103":{"body":"","breadcrumbs":"Arrays » Creating Arrays","id":"103","title":"Creating Arrays"},"104":{"body":"Create an array of a specific size using new T[size]: var numbers = new int[5]; // int[5] — five zeros\\nvar names = new string[3]; // string[3] — three nulls","breadcrumbs":"Arrays » With new","id":"104","title":"With new"},"105":{"body":"Array literals use bracket syntax. An interface declares method signatures and property signatures without providing implementations — any type that lists the interface in its base clause must supply concrete implementations for every member. Interfaces enable polymorphism: code can accept any type that implements a given interface without knowing the concrete type at compile time. An interface is its own type. When a concrete type declares that it implements an interface, it establishes a nominal relationship — the type is-a instance of that interface type. Once something is allocated it is that type forever. Strong - An alias to an object is always typed. You can only perform actions that are comptime provable on the object. The type of the alias must be comptime provable. There is no free casting like C#, there is no any type like Typescript. You can only interact with the information that you’ve proven is valid at that point in time. Kinds - Mist supports the follow kinds Concrete Types - Struct - Value type. Pass by value. Lives directly at the address behind the alias; could be the stack or within another object. Class - Reference type. Pass by reference. It’s alias is a pointer to it’s location. Enum - A reaonly named list of objects associated to a nominal type. The enum is a type itself and has a nominal parent. This is significantly more powerful than it’s C# cousin. Abstract Types - Interface - Nominal types that provide a contract an implement is guarenteed to have met. Trait - Structural types that provide a shape that an implementer has met. This is not the same as it’s Rust counterpart. Significant Features Ownership — A tiered ownership system that tracks how values are shared and mutated, catching use-after-move and aliasing errors at compile time. Type Aliases — Transparent alternative names for existing types ( type Name = ExistingType;) that the compiler erases during transpilation. Values of the alias and the underlying type are fully interchangeable without casts. Newtypes — Distinct types that wrap an existing type ( type Name = new SourceType;). Unlike aliases, newtypes are opaque — you cannot pass a UserId where a plain int is expected without an explicit cast, giving compile-time type safety for domain concepts without runtime overhead. Type Unions — First-class union types ( A | B) that let a value hold one of several types, narrowed safely via pattern matching. Refinement Types — Types constrained by predicates (e.g., int where > 0) that are enforced at compile time and runtime boundaries. Dependent Types — Types parameterized by a compile-time constant value rather than another type (e.g., FixedBuffer<Size:int>), creating a family of distinct types indexed by that value. A FixedBuffer<5> and a FixedBuffer<10> are incompatible types, giving compile-time guarantees about dimensions and capacities. Null Removed — Mist eliminates null entirely. Every type must have a well-defined default value (0 for numerics, \\"\\" for strings, a fully-initialized instance for classes and structs). The default keyword and optional default blocks let types specify their zero-state, removing null-reference errors by construction. Associated Types — Abstract type slots declared inside interfaces and traits whose concrete definition is provided by implementors. Where generic type parameters are chosen by the caller, associated types are chosen by the implementor — enabling patterns like zero-allocation iteration where the compiler resolves the concrete enumerator struct statically, eliminating boxing and virtual dispatch. Structured Context — A mechanism for passing values through a call chain without threading them as explicit parameters, using a per-type context stack and with clauses. The compiler statically verifies that every required context value is available at each call site, giving the ergonomics of dependency injection with compile-time safety.","breadcrumbs":"Introduction » The Language","id":"2","title":"The Language"},"20":{"body":"Create a file called Program.mist with the following code: Mist Emitted C# using Standard; namespace Hello; public class Program\\n{ public static void Main(string[] args) { Console.WriteLine(\\"Hello, World!\\"); }\\n} using System; namespace Hello; public class Program\\n{ public static void Main(string[] args) { System.Console.WriteLine(\\"Hello, World!\\"); } public static Program __CreateDefault() { var inst = new Program(); return inst; }\\n}","breadcrumbs":"Hello, World! » Writing the Program","id":"20","title":"Writing the Program"},"200":{"body":"Extensions are called using dot-notation on an instance of the receiver type, exactly like regular instance members. Where generic type parameters are chosen by the caller of a generic function or constructor, associated types are chosen by the implementor of an interface. This distinction makes associated types ideal for contracts where the implementing type determines a related type that callers shouldn’t need to specify explicitly. The primary motivating use case is zero-allocation iteration: an Iterable<TValue> interface declares an associated enumerator type slot, and each collection provides its own concrete struct enumerator. A refinement type narrows an existing base type by attaching a predicate — only values satisfying that predicate belong to the refined type. This gives you compile-time rejection of invalid values and runtime validation via pattern matching, without writing manual guard code. Unlike type aliases (which are transparent names) or newtypes (which create distinct wrapper types), refinement types keep the same underlying representation as their base type but restrict which values are valid. Refinement predicates use the same clause syntax as pattern matching — relational operators, and combinators, and property patterns. An owned value is the sole, unique reference to its entire object graph — no other binding aliases it, and no one can mutate it behind your back. The compiler tracks ownership at every point in your program and rejects code that would create a second owner or use a value after it has been given away. The defining idea is that ownership is a property of a binding, not of a type. Any non-substructural type — whether it is a plain class, a struct, or a type the author marked owned — can be held in an owned binding and gain unique-ownership tracking. You do not need to design a type up front to participate in ownership; you opt in at the point where you declare the variable. The entire system is compile-time. Ownership annotations are erased in the emitted C# — there is no reference counting, no runtime state, and no hidden allocations. After a move, reading, writing, passing, or taking a reference to the moved binding produces a use-after-move error that names the binding, where it was moved, and where the invalid access happened. Moves interact with control flow. If a binding is moved in one branch of a conditional but not another, it is treated as moved at the join point after the conditional. Add a [global_usings] section to your mist.toml with a namespaces array listing the namespaces you want imported everywhere: # mist.toml\\nname = \\"MyProject\\"\\nnamespace_root = \\"MyProject\\" [global_usings]\\nnamespaces = [\\"MyProject.Models\\", \\"MyProject.Services\\"] With this configuration, every .mist file in the project can reference types from MyProject.Models and MyProject.Services by simple name without writing using declarations: Mist // No explicit using needed — Models and Services are globally imported\\nnamespace MyProject; class Program\\n{ public static void Main() { var user = new User(\\"Alice\\"); // User is in MyProject.Models var svc = new UserService(); // UserService is in MyProject.Services }\\n} A few things to keep in mind: Project-scoped only. Global usings apply exclusively to the project that declares them. If project A references project B, project A does not inherit project B’s global usings. ./book/src/advanced/ownership.md:105:An `owned` type additionally enforces a **field-type restriction**: every field must have a type that is another `owned type`, implements `IClonable<T>`, or is a value type. ./book/src/advanced/default-keyword.md:318:## Abstract Types and Traits
./book/src/advanced/default-keyword.md:320:Abstract types and traits are always non-defaultable. They represent abstract contracts, not concrete values. You cannot call `default(ISerializable)` or `default(Printable)` — the compiler emits `MIST_DEFAULT_ON_INTERFACE` or `MIST_DEFAULT_ON_TRAIT` respectively.
./book/src/advanced/default-keyword.md:322:A `where T : default` constraint will also reject abstract type and trait types as type arguments, since they cannot satisfy the defaultability requirement.

./book/src/object-model/traits.md:1:# Traits
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:3:> **Design Note:** Traits are an area of active design exploration. The core capabilities — structural typing and late binding via `with` — are desired, but the boundary between traits and abstract types is not yet fully resolved. It's unclear when a developer should reach for a trait vs. an abstract type, and whether both need to coexist as separate concepts or could be unified into a single mechanism with optional structural matching. This chapter documents the current design, which may change.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:5:Traits define structural typing contracts. Unlike abstract types, which require a class to explicitly declare conformance, a trait is satisfied by any type whose public members match the trait's declared signatures. This gives you the flexibility of duck typing with the safety of compile-time verification — if a type has the right shape, it fits the trait automatically.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:7:## Trait Declaration
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:9:A trait is declared with the `trait` keyword followed by a name and a body containing field signatures, method signatures, and property signatures. Traits can also extend other traits using the colon syntax.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:14:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/declaration.mist}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:19:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/declaration.cs}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:24:A trait emits as a C# interface. Field signatures in the trait become read-only properties (`{ get; }`) on the emitted interface. Method signatures emit as interface method declarations.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:26:Traits can extend other traits, inheriting all member requirements from their parents:
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:31:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/extending.mist}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:36:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/extending.cs}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:41:A type satisfying `ReadWriteStream` must provide `Read()`, `Write(string)`, and `Flush()` — all members from the trait and its parents.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:45:A type satisfies a trait when its public members match the trait's declared signatures by name and type. No explicit `: TraitName` clause is needed — the compiler verifies structural compatibility at compile time. There are two forms of satisfaction: structural binding and late binding.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:49:Direct binding occurs when a type's members match the trait's signatures exactly — same names, same types. The compiler detects this automatically with no additional declarations:
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:54:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/structural-satisfaction.mist}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:59:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/structural-satisfaction.cs}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:64:The `User` class never mentions `Printable` in its declaration, yet the compiler determines it satisfies the trait. The class's `Name` and `Id` properties match the trait's field signatures, so the structural contract is fulfilled.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:66:If a type is missing a required member, the compiler reports an error at the point where the type is used as the trait type.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:70:Late binding allows a type to satisfy a trait when it has members with compatible types but different names. A `with` block provides explicit member mapping — telling the compiler which member on the type corresponds to which member on the trait. The type doesn't need to be modified, and this is still a compile-time guarantee.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:75:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/with-block-fields.mist}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:80:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/with-block-fields.cs}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:85:The `with` block syntax is `with TypeName : TraitName { sourceMember as traitMember; }`. Each mapping declares that the type's `sourceMember` fulfills the trait's `traitMember`.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:92:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/with-block-methods.mist}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:97:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/with-block-methods.cs}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:102:Here `Logger.Log` is mapped to `Writable.Write`. The key property of late binding is retroactive conformance — you can adapt existing types to new traits without touching the original type's source code.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:106:You can also explicitly list a trait in a type's base clause, just like an abstract type. When you do this, the compiler enforces that the type satisfies the trait — it must have all the required members with matching names and types. This turns the structural check into a hard requirement at the declaration site rather than deferring it to the point of use.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:109:trait Transformable<T> {
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:120:This is useful when you want the compiler to catch missing members immediately rather than waiting until the type is passed somewhere expecting the trait. The type still satisfies the trait structurally — the explicit declaration just makes the intent visible and the error location predictable.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:124:Trait types can be used as variable types and parameter types, accepting any value whose type satisfies the trait — whether through structural matching or a `with` block.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:129:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/polymorphic-usage.mist}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:134:{{#include ../../snippets/object-model/traits/polymorphic-usage.cs}}
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:141:## Traits vs Interfaces
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:143:Traits and abstract types both define contracts, but they differ in how conformance is established:
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:145:| | Traits | Abstract Types |
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:147:| **Typing** | Structural — a type satisfies a trait if its members match | Nominal — a class must explicitly list the abstract type |
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:148:| **Declaration** | No `: TraitName` needed on the class | Requires `: AbstractTypeName` in the class header |
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:150:| **Emitted C#** | Interface + compiler-inserted `: TraitName` on satisfying types | Interface + developer-declared `: AbstractTypeName` |
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:151:| **Retroactive conformance** | Yes — existing types can satisfy new traits without modification | No — the class source must be changed to add the abstract type |
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:153:The key advantage of traits is **retroactive conformance**: you can define a new trait and existing types will satisfy it automatically if they already have the right members. With abstract types, you'd need to modify each class to add the abstract type to its base clause. The `with` block extends this further — even types with differently-named members can be adapted to a trait without touching the original class.
./book/src/object-model/traits.md:155:Both traits and abstract types emit as C# interfaces in the generated code. The difference is purely in how the Mist compiler determines and enforces conformance at compile time.
./book/src/object-model/readonly.md:24:| Trait | All members are implicitly readonly; implementors must satisfy the contract |
./book/src/object-model/target-typed-new.md:112:**Traits** — you cannot instantiate a trait:
./book/src/object-model/target-typed-new.md:115:Printable p = new();  // Error: Cannot create an instance of trait type 'Printable' with target-typed new.

./book/src/type-system/generics.md:77:## Generic Traits
./book/src/type-system/generics.md:79:Traits can declare type parameters with the same syntax. A type satisfies a generic trait when its members match the trait's signatures with the type parameter substituted.
./book/src/type-system/generics.md:84:{{#include ../../snippets/type-system/generics/traits.mist}}
./book/src/type-system/generics.md:89:{{#include ../../snippets/type-system/generics/traits.cs}}
./book/src/type-system/refinement-types.md:201:### Abstract Type and Trait Contracts
./book/src/type-system/associated-types.md:3:Associated types let abstract types and traits declare abstract type slots — type members whose concrete definition is deferred to implementors. Where generic type parameters are chosen by the *caller* of a generic function or constructor, associated types are chosen by the *implementor* of an abstract type. This distinction makes associated types ideal for contracts where the implementing type determines a related type that callers shouldn't need to specify explicitly.
./book/src/type-system/associated-types.md:9:An associated type slot is declared inside an abstract type or trait body using the `type Name : ConstraintList;` syntax. The colon and constraint list specify what the concrete type must satisfy, using the same constraint syntax as generic `where` clauses (see [Generic Constraints](./generic-constraints.md)).
./book/src/type-system/associated-types.md:62:The constraint list supports the same forms as generic constraints: `struct`, `class`, abstract type references, trait references, base class references, `new()`, and combinations thereof.
./book/src/type-system/associated-types.md:64:### Trait Slots
./book/src/type-system/associated-types.md:66:Traits can also declare associated type slots with the same syntax. A type structurally conforming to the trait must provide the required nested type:
./book/src/type-system/associated-types.md:71:{{#include ../../snippets/type-system/associated-types/trait-slot.mist}}
./book/src/type-system/associated-types.md:76:{{#include ../../snippets/type-system/associated-types/trait-slot.cs}}
./book/src/type-system/associated-types.md:81:The emitted C# is identical in shape — traits emit as C# interfaces, and the associated type slot becomes a type parameter with the same constraint propagation.
./book/src/type-system/dependent-types.md:128:## Dependent Types on Traits
./book/src/type-system/dependent-types.md:130:Traits can also declare dependent type parameters. A type satisfies a dependent trait structurally — it must have matching members regardless of the dependent value.
./book/src/type-system/dependent-types.md:135:{{#include ../../snippets/type-system/dependent-types/traits.mist}}
./book/src/type-system/dependent-types.md:140:{{#include ../../snippets/type-system/dependent-types/traits.cs}}
./book/src/type-system/dependent-types.md:145:The trait `ISized<N:int>` declares a contract parameterized by a constant. `SizedBox<N:int>` satisfies it structurally because it provides a `GetCapacity()` method with the correct signature.
./book/src/type-system/generic-constraints.md:15:The constraint can be a type name (abstract type, trait, base class), a structural constraint (`class`, `struct`), or a constructor constraint (`new()`). Multiple constraints on the same type parameter are separated by commas.
./book/src/type-system/generic-constraints.md:74:## Trait Constraint
./book/src/type-system/generic-constraints.md:76:Traits can also be used as constraints. A type satisfies a trait constraint if it structurally matches the trait's members (or has an explicit `with` mapping). The compiler emits the trait as an interface constraint in C#.
./book/src/type-system/generic-constraints.md:81:{{#include ../../snippets/type-system/generic-constraints/trait-constraint.mist}}
./book/src/type-system/generic-constraints.md:86:{{#include ../../snippets/type-system/generic-constraints/trait-constraint.cs}}
./book/src/type-system/generic-constraints.md:91:Any type with a public `string Describe()` method structurally satisfies the `Describable` trait and can be used as `T` in `Describer<T>`.
./book/src/type-system/generic-constraints.md:245:The same `where` clause syntax works uniformly across classes, structs, abstract types, and traits.
./book/src/type-system/generic-constraints.md:254:| `TraitName` | Must structurally satisfy the trait |
./book/src/type-system/generic-constraints.md:260:Constraints compose freely — combine `class`, abstract type, trait, base class, and constructor constraints on the same type parameter to express precise requirements. Use multiple `where` clauses when constraining different type parameters independently.
./book/src/introduction.md:25:    - **Trait** - Structural types that provide a shape that an implementer has met. This is not the same as it's Rust counterpart. 
./book/src/introduction.md:36:- **Associated Types** — Abstract type slots declared inside abstract types and traits whose concrete definition is provided by implementors. Where generic type parameters are chosen by the caller, associated types are chosen by the implementor — enabling patterns like zero-allocation iteration where the compiler resolves the concrete enumerator struct statically, eliminating boxing and virtual dispatch.
./book/src/introduction.md:70:- **Object Model** — Classes, inheritance, structs, properties, abstract types, traits, enums, overloading, and extension methods.
